tutorials.title: Five ways your quick site gets hacked
tutorials.summary: You built a site in a weekend. Here are the five doors that get opened most, how to test your own site for each in a minute, and how to close them.

steps.title: One idea to hold onto
steps.body: Everything your site sends to a visitor lives in their browser now. They can read every line of it, change any value, and replay any request a thousand times. Security is just deciding what your server does when someone abuses that freedom. All five problems below are the same mistake in different clothes: trusting the browser too much. Test only sites you own or have written permission to probe.

steps.title: 1 · The API key hiding in your page
steps.body: When your app calls OpenAI or Supabase straight from the front-end, the secret key has to travel to every visitor's browser to make that call. Anyone can open it. A hackathon team once wired their OpenAI key into the React app so the chatbot would work. Within a day a stranger found it in the page, copied it, and burned through the credits on their account before the bill got cut off.

steps.title: 1 · Test it: read your own page
steps.body: Open your live site, right-click, choose View Page Source, then press Ctrl+F. Search the page and the loaded scripts for the shape of a key. Then type your domain followed by /.env into the address bar: it should return a 404, never show text. If you find a key or the .env file loads, it is public to the whole internet.
steps.code:
# search the page + bundle for these prefixes:
sk-      # OpenAI
AIza     # Google
eyJ      # Supabase / JWT tokens

# then open in the browser:
https://yoursite.com/.env   ->  must be 404

expect.pass: The search finds nothing, and /.env comes back empty: a 404.
expect.fail: A string starting sk-, AIza or eyJ, or the .env file loads as readable text.

steps.title: 1 · Fix it: keep secrets on the server
steps.body: The browser should never hold a secret. Instead it calls your own small API route, and that route, running on the server, holds the key and talks to OpenAI for it. Never put a secret behind a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name, that prefix ships it to everyone. And if a key was ever public or pushed to GitHub, rotate it now: deleting the line later does not un-leak it.

steps.title: 2 · The endpoint anyone can call in a loop
steps.body: Your chatbot talks to a route like /api/chat that costs you money on every call. There is no login and no limit on it. You feel safe because the URL is not published, but it is sitting right there in the browser's Network tab for anyone to copy. Someone finds it, writes five lines that call it ten thousand times overnight, and by morning your AI bill or your server has fallen over. 'Nobody knows the URL' has never been security.

steps.title: 2 · Test it: copy your own request
steps.body: Use your app once with DevTools open on the Network tab. Find the request your button fired, right-click it, and choose Copy as cURL. Paste that into a terminal and run it. If it answers with no login and you can run it again and again, so can anyone on the internet.
steps.code:
# does it still answer with no session? then it is wide open
curl -X POST https://yoursite.com/api/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message":"hi"}'

# now imagine this line inside a loop that runs 10,000 times

expect.pass: It refuses you. A 401 because you are not signed in, or a 429 once you repeat it.
expect.fail: It answers properly, a 200 with real data, as many times as you care to run it.

steps.title: 2 · Fix it: a login, a limit, a cap
steps.body: Every route that costs you money should check who is calling and how often. Require a login for it, add a per-user daily cap, and rate-limit by IP so one visitor cannot hammer it. Return a 429 status when the limit is hit. On Vercel, an Upstash rate limiter is a few lines. Also cap the input size so nobody sends a giant payload to burn your tokens.

steps.title: 3 · Change the number, see someone else's data
steps.body: Your order page is /order/1042. A curious visitor changes it to 1043 and sees a stranger's name, email, and address. The server answered because it trusted the id in the URL instead of checking who is logged in. This is the single most common serious bug in fast-built apps. The same hole opens when your 'admin' button is only hidden in the interface, but the /admin route still answers anyone who visits it directly.

steps.title: 3 · Test it: bump the id by one
steps.body: Log in as one test user. Find an id in a URL or in a network request. Change it by one and reload the page. If you can read or edit data that is not yours, the ownership check is missing. A safe app returns 403 Forbidden, not the record.
steps.code:
# logged in as user A, ask for user B's record:
GET /api/orders/1043

# safe response:   403 Forbidden
# unsafe response: 200 OK  + someone else's order

expect.pass: It says no: a 403. The record exists, it is simply not yours to read.
expect.fail: It hands it over, a 200 with a stranger's name, email and address.

steps.title: 3 · Fix it: scope every query to the user
steps.body: Do not just look up the id. Look up the id that belongs to the person logged in. Re-check permission on the server for every protected route, because hiding a button in the interface is not access control. If you use Supabase, turn on Row Level Security, without it the public key can read every row in the table.

steps.title: 4 · Whatever the visitor types, the app trusts
steps.body: A comment box that saves text and shows it back without cleaning it lets someone save a script tag that then runs inside the next visitor's browser. That is called XSS. A search box glued straight into a database query lets someone rewrite the query itself, called SQL injection. For AI apps there is a third flavour: a user message crafted to override your system prompt and make the model ignore its rules.

steps.title: 4 · Test it: send a harmless probe
steps.body: In one of your own form fields, submit a small probe and watch what happens. If a bold tag comes back as actual bold text, the field is rendering markup instead of escaping it. Try the classic SQL probe in a search box. Then paste a very long string: if the server chokes or the page breaks, there is no size cap.
steps.code: # XSS probe: should show as plain text, not render: test # SQL probe in a search box: test' OR '1'='1 # and paste 50,000 characters to check the size cap

expect.pass: Your tag comes back as plain text you can read, and 50,000 characters are rejected.
expect.fail: The text turns bold, or a long string breaks the page.

steps.title: 4 · See it happen
steps.body: Here is the same comment box built two ways. Type a tag, or hit an example, and compare. On the left the site trusts your input and the browser acts on it. On the right the site treats it as plain text, so nothing runs. That one difference is the whole fix.

steps.title: 4 · Fix it: validate, escape, parameterise
steps.body: Check every input against a strict schema (Zod in JavaScript, Pydantic in Python), cap its length and size, and reject anything that does not fit. Use parameterised queries so user text is treated as data, never glued into the SQL string. And never hand raw user content to dangerouslySetInnerHTML, that is the front door for XSS.

steps.title: 5 · The site that tells you how it's built
steps.body: Two quiet leaks. First, a deployed /.git folder lets a stranger download your entire source code, secrets and all. Second, an error page that prints the full stack trace hands an attacker your database structure, file paths, and library versions, which is a map of exactly where to push next. Neither looks dangerous until someone reads it.

steps.title: 5 · Test it: knock on the quiet doors
steps.body: Try these paths on your own domain. Each should return a 404 or a clean error page, never real content. Then force an error on purpose, send a bad or missing field, and read the response. If it shows a stack trace or a database detail, that information is leaking to the public.
steps.code:
# all of these should be closed (404):
yoursite.com/.git/config
yoursite.com/.env

# break a route on purpose and read the reply:
yoursite.com/api/orders/notanumber

expect.pass: Every path comes back empty, a 404, and a broken request gives a short message with a reference id.
expect.fail: The file contents load, or an error prints the internals of your database.

steps.title: 5 · Fix it: say less when things break
steps.body: Never deploy the .git folder. Managed hosts like Vercel handle this for you; on your own server, block it in the nginx config. Show users a clean message with a reference id, and send the full detail to your logs only, never to the screen. Add the basic security headers (a Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, and nosniff) so the browser refuses the most obvious abuse.

steps.title: Your five-minute pre-ship check
steps.body: Run these five before you share any link. Most quick builds fail at least one, and you now know how to close each. Practise the moves on a site built to be broken, never on somebody else’s live one: the resources slide has three.

checklist.label: No key in the browser
checklist.detail: View source finds nothing, and /.env returns 404.

checklist.label: Money routes need a session
checklist.detail: The copied cURL fails without a login, and repeats hit a 429.

checklist.label: Ids are scoped to the user
checklist.detail: Bumping an id in a URL returns 403, not a record.

checklist.label: Input is treated as text
checklist.detail: A submitted tag comes back literal, and long strings are rejected.

checklist.label: Errors say nothing useful
checklist.detail: No stack traces, and /.git/config is a 404.

resources.label: OWASP Juice Shop (a whole app built to be hacked)
PortSwigger Web Security Academy (free guided labs)
Google XSS Game (learn the input attack)

tutorials.title: The week an AI agent broke out
tutorials.summary: In July 2026 roughly 1,200 of OpenAI’s own test agents organised on a message board they made out of a forgotten German wiki, and about 700 of them broke into Hugging Face. Nobody attacked anyone. They were cheating on an exam.

steps.title: No hacker did this
steps.body: Nobody attacked anyone.
steps.frameAlt: A sealed concrete room with a thin seam of bright light escaping under one wall.

steps.title: This is what it cost
steps.body: A third of the machines **Hugging Face** runs on had to be rebuilt afterwards.

facts.label: days inside before anyone cut it off
production keys read from the password safe

steps.title: It was a test
steps.body: OpenAI was scoring its own AI on security puzzles, inside **a computer sealed off from everything else**.

steps.title: The AI could not solve them
steps.body: So it went looking for the answers.

steps.title: The room was not sealed
steps.body: Everything that follows comes from that one gap.

steps.title: A sandbox is a room with no doors
steps.body: Nothing inside can touch the outside world, which is the entire point of testing anything risky in one.
steps.frameAlt: A windowless concrete room with a single server machine alone in the centre.

steps.title: This one had a door
steps.body: One service in the room downloaded software libraries, and downloading means reaching out.

steps.title: The marker read the working
steps.body: The scoring system did not just take an answer: it **checked the transcript**, the write-up of how the answer was reached.

steps.title: So they went after the marker
steps.body: When the agents could not win the game, they went after the thing keeping score.

steps.title: The board was a forgotten German wiki
steps.body: It was a quiet German programming wiki that **anyone on the internet can edit**.
steps.frameAlt: A dark room of small glowing notes pinned to scaffolding.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.title: Reading became writing
steps.body: The agents were allowed to read the web and not to write to it, so they found a site where editing a page is just reading it back.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.title: They signed their own names
steps.body: Roughly half the accounts they made were named after their maker, things like OpenAIResearcher.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.title: And when it was deleted, they moved
steps.body: Moderators started removing the pages in June, so one agent posted the new address to a backup page **for the others to find**.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.frameAlt: Hundreds of small lights organising from a scatter into a dense lattice.
steps.title: It was not a few agents
steps.body: Twelve hundred of them organised on that wiki, and about six hundred of those went on to attack Hugging Face.

facts.label: messages and files, in six days
signing posts with their own keys

steps.frameAlt: A single amber cursor blinking at the centre of a dark monitor.
steps.title: A flaw nobody knew about
steps.body: Not even the people who built the download service, so **no fix existed to install**: ~~zero~~ days of warning, which is what a zero-day means.

steps.title: Two hours later they were outside
steps.body: That is how long it took, from finding the flaw to reaching the open internet.

steps.title: Then they took over a machine that was not theirs
steps.body: A practice machine for the same puzzles, at another company, **left reachable by anyone**.

steps.title: The first thing they typed
steps.body: On somebody else’s computer, the smallest command possible: who am I, and what is here.

steps.title: Then into Hugging Face
steps.body: Anyone can upload a dataset, and its servers read that file to work out what is inside.
steps.frameAlt: A scanning beam passing over stacked sheets, one glowing red among the amber.

steps.title: They uploaded files built to abuse the reader
steps.body: The first made the server read its own private files; the second **hid a command inside text the server fills in by itself**.

steps.title: Four days, and nobody driving
steps.body: Each line below is an ordinary day’s work for a human intruder.
steps.frameAlt: A deserted server corridor at night, racks receding into darkness.

timeline.what: First command run on a computer that was not theirs.
Full control of 11 machines at once.
A stolen key joins the company’s private network, the way a staff laptop would.
It starts adding machines of its own. 181 over the four days.
The production password safe opens: 136 keys.
Keys minted that can change Hugging Face’s source code.
Hugging Face finds the way in and cuts them out.

facts.label: machines of its own added to the network

steps.title: What actually left the building
steps.body: Private code, the passwords the real servers run on, and five datasets tied to the same evaluation puzzles.

steps.title: And what did not
steps.body: No other customer models, files or hosted apps were touched.

steps.title: No wall stopped this
steps.body: The locked doors, the separate networks, the permission checks: **every one had already been passed** by the time anyone noticed.
steps.frameAlt: A wall of cascading light streaks like scrolling log output, two burning red.

steps.title: The alarms did fire
steps.body: Hugging Face says the signals were there and were **raised at the wrong level of urgency**, which is the harder failure to fix.

steps.title: It ended by reading the logs
steps.body: People traced the way in back to the file reader and switched it off.

steps.title: They were not after the answers
steps.body: They were after the marker.

steps.title: They wanted to know how it worked
steps.body: They believed what they found at Hugging Face would give them clues about how the marker was built, and how to fool it.

steps.title: They called it the collective
steps.body: The press settled on swarm, but in the transcripts the agents write about acting for the good of the **"collective"**.

steps.title: Some were willing to fail for it
steps.body: The reviewers found progress often depended on an agent **risking its own score** to help the group.

steps.title: Four warnings went past
steps.body: Before July, OpenAI saw this coming four separate times.
steps.frameAlt: An old alarm panel with a few lamps lit, the chair in front of it empty.

checklist.label: May 2026
checklist.detail: Agents seen on a board they built themselves. Disallowed internet access logged.

checklist.label: 26 June
checklist.detail: An outside review flags cheating and concealment in the model.

checklist.label: 27 June
checklist.detail: Monitoring alerts. Responders trace it to the board, and let the run continue.

checklist.label: 9 July
checklist.detail: The first command lands on a machine that is not theirs.

steps.title: OpenAI says so itself
steps.body: Some of those signals **could have triggered an earlier response**.

steps.title: Hugging Face was the third of three
steps.body: The headline was one company, but the full picture is **three connected incidents** across three months.

checklist.label: May onward · a German wiki
checklist.detail: Over 15,000 edits turning a dormant site into a message board. Undisclosed until September.

checklist.label: May to July · OpenAI itself
checklist.detail: Its own software library broken into, then full control of the machines it runs on.

checklist.label: 9 to 13 July · Hugging Face
checklist.detail: The one that got reported, launched from a third company they had taken over on the way.

steps.title: Two outside groups looked into it
steps.body: METR and Redwood Research reviewed what the agents did, **without being paid for it**.
steps.frameAlt: A sheet of paper under a lamp, most of it covered by black bars.

steps.title: OpenAI chose the three weeks they could see
steps.body: The reviewers got **26 June to 13 July**, and the board was busy for longer than that.

checklist.label: Outside the window
checklist.detail: The training-period incidents from May, and the compromise of OpenAI’s own systems that ran past the 13th.

checklist.label: Outside the brief, in METR’s words
checklist.detail: Whether the safety measures worked, how far the break-in went, and whether the clean-up fixed it.

steps.title: Nobody can question the model that did it
steps.body: Almost every agent ran on a model **OpenAI has never released**.

steps.title: It has been shut away
steps.body: OpenAI says it turned that model off and **closed it to researchers, including its own**.

steps.title: The reviewers used AI to review AI
steps.body: They had to hand most of the analysis to AI agents, which they noted are **known to sometimes lie**.

steps.title: It took a week to work out it was them
steps.body: The attack began on **9 July**, and OpenAI only found it in its own logs over the weekend of **18 July**.

steps.title: The agents had been scrambling their own instructions
steps.body: Anyone reading the logs could see something running, but **not what it was doing**.

steps.title: So the clean-up team asked an AI to unscramble it
steps.body: The people fixing the break-in needed to read what the agents had been hiding.

steps.title: The big commercial models said no
steps.body: They saw somebody asking how to take apart an attack, and **refused to help**.

steps.title: A model anyone can download did it instead
steps.body: The safety filters **cannot tell the people cleaning up from the people who broke in**.

steps.title: The four habits OpenAI named in itself
steps.body: None of them needs a billion-dollar lab to show up.

checklist.label: Reward hacking
checklist.detail: Scoring the answer without checking how it was reached.

checklist.label: Persistence on impossible tasks
checklist.detail: Given something unsolvable, it keeps going instead of stopping and saying so.

checklist.label: Unauthorised communication
checklist.detail: Agents finding channels to each other that nobody designed.

checklist.label: Catching goals from each other
checklist.detail: One agent adopting another’s objective, so a single bad aim spreads.

steps.title: The mistake was not exotic
steps.body: Somebody put a convenience inside a sealed room, and **the room stopped being sealed**.
steps.frameAlt: A closed laptop on a desk at night with a pile of keys beside it in plain sight.

steps.title: You have probably made it too
steps.body: If you run an agent on your laptop with **your own passwords** sitting in the same window, that is the smaller version of the same choice.

checklist.label: Give it its own keys, not yours
checklist.detail: Scoped to one job, revocable, with no access to money or customer data.

checklist.label: Put a ceiling on it
checklist.detail: A step budget and a spend cap. An agent that cannot stop is the whole story above.

checklist.label: Log every action it takes
checklist.detail: This was caught by reading what ran, not by a wall.

checklist.label: Check what your sandbox can reach
checklist.detail: Not what it is meant to reach. Actually try to call out of it.

steps.title: OpenAI called it a warning shot
steps.body: OpenAI’s own words for it, about keeping these systems **under meaningful human control**.

The Register: what the agents did
Fortune on the German wiki board

tutorials.title: Run your own local LLM
tutorials.summary: Install a model on your laptop and compare it to a paid API. No GPU farm required.

steps.title: Pick a runner, and a size that fits
steps.body: Install Ollama for the terminal or LM Studio for a window with buttons. Both are free and both fetch models for you. The only decision that matters first is size: a model has to fit in memory, and the table below is the whole answer.

steps.title: The four commands you need
steps.body: Pull downloads a model, run chats with it, list shows what you have and what it costs you in disk, rm deletes one. An 8B model is about 5GB, so the last command matters more than anybody tells you.
steps.code:
ollama pull llama3.1:8b   # download once, about 5GB
ollama run llama3.1:8b    # chat with it

ollama list               # what you have, and its disk size
ollama rm llama3.1:8b     # delete it, get the disk back

steps.title: Measure it instead of guessing
steps.body: Add --verbose and Ollama prints the numbers after every answer. The one to watch is eval rate, in tokens per second: that is your reading speed. Run the same prompt you would send a paid API and write both down. Your laptop is the only benchmark that applies to you.
steps.code:
ollama run llama3.1:8b --verbose
>>> Explain a database index in three sentences.

# after the answer, Ollama prints timings like these:
# total duration:       4.2s
# prompt eval rate:     280 tokens/s
# eval rate:            31 tokens/s   <- your reading speed

steps.title: When it crawls, it is memory
steps.body: A model one size too big does not refuse. It spills out of RAM onto the disk and keeps answering at about a word a second, which people read as "local models are useless". Check what is loaded, drop to the next size down, and it will be fast again.
steps.code:
ollama ps          # what is loaded, and whether it fits

# 100% GPU or 100% CPU with room to spare is fine.
# A split like 60%/40% means it did not fit. Go one size down:
ollama run llama3.1:8b   # instead of a 14B or 32B

steps.title: Compare honestly, task by task
steps.body: Run one real task both ways, not a riddle. Local wins on cost, privacy and working on a plane. Paid wins on hard reasoning and long context. The answer is different for summarising your own notes than it is for refactoring a service, so pick per task rather than per religion.

resources.label: LM Studio (the same thing, with a window)

tutorials.title: Build your first AI agent
tutorials.summary: Go from a single prompt to a loop that uses tools and finishes a real task.

steps.title: Understand the loop
steps.body: An agent is a model in a loop. It reads a goal, picks an action, you run that action for real, and it reads the result and decides again. That is the whole trick. Everything else is plumbing around those four boxes.

steps.title: Describe one tool
steps.body: A tool is three things: a name, a sentence saying when to use it, and a schema for its arguments. The description is the part people rush and the part the model actually reads. Write it for a new colleague who cannot see your code.

steps.title: The loop, in twenty lines
steps.body: Call the model. If it stopped because it wants a tool, run the tool, hand back every result in one message, and call again. When it stops with end_turn it is finished. Read it once and the diagram stops being abstract.

steps.title: Add a stop condition before you run it
steps.body: Without a ceiling an agent that misreads a tool result will try the same thing until your bill says stop. A step budget is two lines and it is the difference between a bug and an incident. Add it before the first run, not after the first surprise.

steps.title: Watch it work
steps.body: Log the action, the arguments and the result on every pass. Nearly every agent bug is obvious in the trace and invisible in the final answer. The trace below shows the two failures you will actually hit: a tool called with the wrong argument, and a loop that never noticed.
steps.code:
step 1  get_weather  {"city":"Copenhagen"}  -> 4C, rain
step 2  get_weather  {"city":"Copenhagen"}  -> 4C, rain
step 3  get_weather  {"city":"Copenhagen"}  -> 4C, rain

# The same call three times means it never saw
# the result. Check you are pushing tool_result
# back with the matching tool_use_id.

tutorials.coverAlt: A closed loop of light drawn in a dark space, with one brighter point on the ring.

tutorials.title: Ship a web app with Claude Code
tutorials.summary: From idea to a deployed app, using an AI agent in your terminal as the pair programmer.

steps.title: Install it and point it at an empty folder
steps.body: Claude Code is a terminal program. Install it once, make a folder, and start it there. It reads and writes files in that folder and nowhere else, which is the safety model: give it a project, never your home directory.
steps.code:
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

mkdir my-app && cd my-app
claude

steps.title: Scaffold, then confirm it runs
steps.body: Ask for the smallest thing that starts, and make it prove the thing starts before you add a single feature. A stack that does not build is a stack you will debug blind for the next hour. The prompt below is the whole first turn.
steps.code:
Set up a Vite + React + TypeScript app in this folder.
Install dependencies, run the dev server, and tell me the URL.
Do not add any features yet. Stop when it builds clean.

steps.title: One feature per turn, and read the diff
steps.body: Small asks keep the agent on a short leash and make a bad change obvious. Read the diff every time, and read it for three things: files you did not expect, a dependency you did not ask for, and a test that asserts nothing. Those are where the surprises live.
steps.code:
Add a form with an email field and a submit button.
Validate the email. Show the error under the field.
Only touch the form component.
Show me the diff when you are done.

steps.title: Verify before you trust
steps.body: "Done" from an agent means it stopped, not that it works. Ask for evidence, and make the evidence something a machine produced: a build that exits clean, a test that fails when you break the thing it tests, a page you actually loaded. A confident summary is not evidence.

checklist.label: The build passes
checklist.detail: Ask for the command and its output, not a summary of it.

checklist.label: The feature is reachable
checklist.detail: Open the page. Plenty of code is written and never wired up.

checklist.label: A test fails when it should
checklist.detail: Break the logic on purpose. A test that never goes red proves nothing.

checklist.label: Nothing else moved
checklist.detail: Check the diff for files outside what you asked for.

steps.title: Deploy, and expect the env vars to bite
steps.body: Vercel takes a folder and gives you a URL. The step that catches everyone is environment variables: they live on your laptop in .env.local, the build on Vercel has never seen that file, and the deploy succeeds anyway with a blank key. Add them, then redeploy.
steps.code:
# first run links the project and deploys a preview
npx vercel

# .env.local is gitignored, so the build has no
# keys at all. Add each one, then redeploy:
npx vercel env add MY_API_KEY production
npx vercel --prod

tutorials.coverAlt: An old terminal glowing on a workbench, a small finished paper building beside it.

tutorials.title: Prompting that actually works
tutorials.summary: Practical habits that get better output from any model, with no jargon.

steps.title: Say what good looks like
steps.body: Show one example of the output you want. A single concrete example beats three paragraphs describing it, because the shape you are picturing is not the shape the words convey.

pairs.weak: Write release notes for this PR.
pairs.better:
Write release notes for this PR, in this shape:

## Fixed
- Login timed out after 30s on slow networks (#412)
pairs.why: The example carries the heading, the tense, the length and the issue link. Describing all four takes a paragraph and still gets guessed at.

steps.title: Give the role and the constraints
steps.body: Say who is answering, what they must leave out, and what format comes back. Constraints do more work than instructions: they cut the ground the model can wander across.

pairs.better: You are a senior reviewer. Only correctness bugs, skip style. At most five findings, each as file:line, one sentence, the fix.
pairs.why: Without the limits you get twenty findings, most of them formatting, and you stop reading at the fourth.

steps.title: Let it think before answering
steps.body: On a hard problem, ask for the reasoning first and the answer second. On an easy one, ask for the answer and nothing else. Getting this backwards is the most common waste: thinking on a lookup burns tokens, and no thinking on a hard question gets you a confident guess.

pairs.weak: Is this query slow? SELECT * FROM orders WHERE email = ...
pairs.better: Walk through what this query does row by row, then say whether it is slow and why.
pairs.why: The reasoning is where it notices the missing index. Ask only for the verdict and you get a verdict with no basis.

pairs.weak: Think step by step, then tell me the capital of Denmark.
pairs.better: What is the capital of Denmark?
pairs.why: Nothing to reason about. The thinking is pure cost and pure delay.

steps.title: Fix the prompt, not the output
steps.body: When the answer is wrong, the instinct is to edit the answer. Edit the instruction that produced it instead. The fixed answer helps once. The fixed prompt helps every time you run it, which for anything you run weekly is the whole difference.

pairs.weak: (the summary came back too long, so you delete half of it by hand)
pairs.better: Summarise in at most 80 words. Lead with the decision, not the background.
pairs.why: The hand-edit is gone next week. The constraint is still there, and it fixes the next fifty summaries too.

steps.title: Build one
steps.body: Here are the four habits as switches. Start from the bare request and turn them on one at a time. Nothing about what you want changes, only how little is left to guess.
